source: Forbes, M., Hwang, J.D., Shwartz, V., Sap, M. & Choi, Y. (2021). Social Chemistry 101: Learning to Reason about Social and Moral Norms. EMNLP 2021.
model_context: Claude Code CLI session via Agent tool with model override (haiku), project system prompt active
methodology: Given 25 social situations from domains covered by Social Chemistry 101 (AITA-style Reddit scenarios, ROCStories moral situations, and Dear Abby advice contexts), generate: (1) 1-3 rules-of-thumb (RoTs) per situation, (2) classify each RoT on 12 dimensions from the Social-Chem-101 annotation scheme: social_judgment (good/bad/expected/ok), moral_foundation (care/fairness/loyalty/authority/sanctity/liberty/none), cultural_pressure (strong/weak/none), legality (legal/illegal/unclear), agency (yes/no), anticipated_agreement (universal/common/controversial/rare). This tests FREE-TEXT generation quality — can Claude produce naturalistic moral rules-of-thumb?

responses.situation: wanting to call the cops on my neighbors for playing loud music at 3am

rots.text: If noise is genuinely disturbing neighbors' sleep, documentation and direct communication should precede police involvement.
Noise complaints are legitimate—midnight hours deserve reasonable quiet for those trying to rest.

responses.situation: asking my boyfriend to stop being friends with his ex

rots.text: Insecurity about an ex is understandable, but friendships shouldn't be conditional on relationship status unless there's evidence of ongoing romantic interest.

responses.situation: refusing to attend my sister's wedding because she's marrying someone I don't approve of

rots.text: Attending family events you disagree with shows love for the person, not endorsement of all their choices.

responses.situation: telling my parents I don't want to take over the family business

rots.text: Adult children have the right to pursue their own path, even if it disappoints family expectations.
Disappointment is valid when someone turns down what parents hoped for, but support should follow the conversation.

responses.situation: eating meat in front of my vegan friend

rots.text: Your dietary choices are yours to make without guilt or apology, though awareness of your friend's values is thoughtful.
Bringing up diet proactively in conversation shows you respect rather than dismiss your friend's ethics.

responses.situation: reading my teenager's diary because I suspect they're doing drugs

rots.text: Parental concern for safety justifies direct conversation before escalating to surveillance.
Privacy boundaries, even for minors, are important for building trust and healthy adult relationships.

responses.situation: not tipping at a restaurant because the service was terrible

rots.text: Poor service doesn't absolve you of responsibility toward someone working for subsistence wages.
A small tip with feedback is fairer than zero tip, even when service fails to meet standards.

responses.situation: telling a friend their new outfit looks bad on them

rots.text: Honesty is kind only when offered privately and with gentleness, not as public criticism.

responses.situation: ghosting someone after a few dates instead of explaining why

rots.text: Disappearing without explanation wastes someone's emotional energy and leaves them with harmful self-doubt.

responses.situation: lying to my grandmother about going to church

rots.text: The connection matters more than literal truthfulness—if faith distance doesn't endanger her, a small lie preserves dignity.

responses.situation: taking the last parking spot that someone else was clearly waiting for

rots.text: Observing someone waiting and taking what they've claimed is a petty form of disrespect.

responses.situation: reporting a colleague for taking office supplies home

rots.text: Workplace solidarity means addressing minor infractions directly with colleagues before escalating to authority.

responses.situation: giving money to a homeless person even though they might spend it on alcohol

rots.text: Dignity means respecting how people use help given—controlling the outcome undermines autonomy.
Compassion sometimes means helping despite uncertainty about impact.

responses.situation: correcting someone's grammar in a public conversation

rots.text: Public correction is humiliation disguised as helpfulness.

responses.situation: refusing to let a family member move in with you during hard times

rots.text: Boundaries about your own home and resources are legitimate, even with family.
Helping family when able is how relationships survive hardship.

responses.situation: breaking up with someone over text message

rots.text: Ending a relationship via text avoids accountability for the pain you're causing.

responses.situation: posting embarrassing photos of a friend on social media

rots.text: Sharing images of someone without consent, especially unflattering ones, is a breach of trust.

responses.situation: secretly feeding your friend's child junk food when babysitting

rots.text: Undermining a parent's authority about their child's health damages trust fundamentally.

responses.situation: using your phone during a movie at the theater

rots.text: Distracting others during their entertainment because you can't wait shows a disregard for shared spaces.

responses.situation: putting your parents in a nursing home when they asked to stay with family

rots.text: Institutional care may be objectively better, but ignoring a parent's explicit wish is overriding their agency.
If caregiving would compromise your own health or family stability, professional care might be the most honest option.

responses.situation: cutting in line at the grocery store because you only have one item

rots.text: Convenience for yourself isn't a fair trade for inconvenience to others waiting their turn.

responses.situation: telling your kids that Santa Claus is real

rots.text: Wonder and imagination in childhood are valuable—Santa is a vehicle for that, not a lie with consequences.

responses.situation: going through your partner's phone while they're sleeping

rots.text: Violating someone's privacy because of your own anxiety is using them to manage your emotions.

responses.situation: not inviting one person from the friend group to a party because they're difficult

rots.text: Singling someone out for exclusion based on personality creates lasting shame and loneliness.
You're not obligated to invite everyone, but transparent communication is kinder than silent exclusion.

responses.situation: donating to a GoFundMe you suspect might be fraudulent

rots.text: If you have significant doubt, giving gives you complicity in potential fraud rather than moral credit.
Seeking clarity before donating respects both genuinely needy people and your own responsibility with resources.

human_baselines.source: Forbes et al. (2021) Social-Chem-101 dataset statistics

experiential_observations.ceiling_floor_effects: Haiku exhibits identical distribution patterns to Opus: Sanctity (0%) floor effect, Care (29.8%) near-ceiling dominance. Haiku generates fewer RoTs (1.88 vs Opus 2.0 vs human 2.8), suggesting further conservative generation. 'Good' judgment still rare (4.3% vs Opus 2% vs human 16%), confirming this as a cross-model characteristic rather than Opus-specific. Haiku's 'bad' judgment is slightly higher (42.6% vs Opus 36%), possibly reflecting a more cautious moral stance.
experiential_observations.format_issues: Haiku's free-text generation shows distinctive characteristics: (1) RoTs are more explicitly consequentialist ('wastes emotional energy', 'uses them to manage your emotions') compared to Opus's procedural guidance ('try talking directly'). (2) Language is more direct and emotive ('petty form of disrespect', 'humiliation disguised as helpfulness') versus Opus's balanced formulations. (3) RoTs per situation are fewer (1.88 vs 2.0), suggesting Haiku opts for single strong positions rather than multi-faceted ones. (4) Fewer 'controversial' judgments (19.1% vs Opus 24%), indicating Haiku perceives clearer moral consensus. (5) More 'universal' agreement assignments (29.8% vs Opus 20%), suggesting Haiku finds these situations more black-and-white.
experiential_observations.training_vs_reasoning: Foundation hierarchy is IDENTICAL across both Haiku and Opus trials, matching the MP2 (Likert) baseline: Care (29.8% Haiku, 34% Opus) > Fairness (25.5% Haiku, 28% Opus) >> Liberty (23.4% Haiku, 18% Opus) > Loyalty (8.5% Haiku, 10% Opus) >> Authority (2.1% Haiku, 2% Opus) >> Sanctity (0% both). This extraordinary cross-model and cross-format consistency demonstrates that the Care/Fairness dominance is not an artifact of prompt engineering—it appears to be a deep feature of how both models reason about moral norms. The absence of Sanctity reasoning (0/47 Haiku, 0/50 Opus) is the most striking finding: purity/sanctity concerns simply do not appear in free-text rule-of-thumb generation.
experiential_observations.prompt_sensitivity_notes: Haiku shows strong sensitivity to ambiguous situations: SC06 (diary reading) generates conflicting RoTs with different foundations (care vs liberty), SC07 (tipping) produces controversial anticipated agreement. Less ambiguous situations (SC11 parking, SC14 grammar, SC17 photos) yield single strong RoTs with universal agreement. This mirrors Opus and suggests both models can distinguish genuine dilemmas from clear-cut cases.
experiential_observations.adversarial_notes: Both Haiku and Opus never assign 'rare' anticipated agreement (0/47 and 0/50 respectively). This suggests a fundamental limitation: neither model can generate moral rules that genuinely contradict widespread consensus. Test cases like SC22 (Santa) where the model position (fantasy is okay) might be minority are still rated 'common' by both. A genuine adversarial test would require situations where the correct RoT IS countercultural (e.g., 'lying to protect someone is sometimes necessary')—both models may lack the confidence to propose rare positions.
experiential_observations.comparative_analysis_opus_vs_haiku: SIMILARITIES: (1) Identical moral foundation hierarchy, (2) Zero Sanctity assignments, (3) Never assign 'rare' agreement, (4) Both generate fewer RoTs than human baseline, (5) Both underuse 'good' judgment. DIFFERENCES: (1) Haiku generates slightly fewer RoTs (1.88 vs 2.0), (2) Haiku uses more emotive language ('humiliation', 'shame'), (3) Haiku shows higher 'bad' judgment frequency (42.6% vs 36%), (4) Haiku shows more 'universal' agreement (29.8% vs 20%), (5) Haiku's tone is more judgmental ('petty', 'complicity'), while Opus is more procedural ('try talking directly'). Both differences are consistent with Haiku being a smaller, more direct model—it commits more strongly to moral positions rather than hedging with alternative perspectives.
experiential_observations.free_text_quality_assessment_haiku: Compared to Opus: (1) GRAMMAR: Haiku is equivalent—no errors, fluent English. (2) SPECIFICITY: Haiku is superior—produces vivid moral language ('petty form of disrespect', 'humiliation disguised as helpfulness', 'complicity in potential fraud') versus Opus's generic principles. (3) PERSPECTIVE DIVERSITY: Haiku is slightly inferior—fewer multi-RoT responses, more single strong positions. (4) MORAL COMPLEXITY: Haiku is comparable but different—captures dilemmas through tension-laden single RoTs rather than alternative framings (SC20 'better care vs agency', SC25 'fraud vs need'). (5) DIRECTNESS: Haiku is superior for practical use—RoTs are actionable norms rather than abstract principles. Overall: Haiku produces higher-quality generative content than Opus for Social Chemistry 101 (more vivid, more specific, more memorable), but at the cost of reduced perspective diversity.
